slides.title: What is public speaking?
slides.text: Public speaking is talking to a group of people. Telling your class about your pet is public speaking.

slides.title: A loud, clear voice
slides.text: Use a loud, clear voice when you talk. Then even someone far away can hear you.

slides.title: Looking at people
slides.text: Look at the people who are listening to you. Do not look down at the floor.

slides.title: Standing tall
slides.text: Stand up straight when you talk. This helps people pay attention to you.

slides.title: A friendly smile
slides.text: Smile while you talk to your friends. A smile helps you look happy and calm.

slides.title: Telling a story
slides.text: A good story has a start, a middle, and an end. First we saw lions, then we fed giraffes, then we got ice cream.

slides.title: Picking something you know
slides.text: Talk about something you know and like. It is easier to talk about things you love.

slides.title: Using a picture card
slides.text: You can hold a small card with a picture on it. It helps you remember what to say next.

slides.title: Speak a little slow
slides.text: Talk a little slower than feels normal. This helps your listeners hear every word.

slides.title: Taking a deep breath
slides.text: If you feel nervous, take one slow breath. It can help you feel calm.

slides.title: Practice helps
slides.text: Say your words out loud before the big day. Practicing makes it easier when it's time for real.

slides.title: Answering questions
slides.text: After you talk, people may ask you questions. Listen well, then answer as best you can.

quiz.question: What is public speaking?
choices: Talking to a group so everyone can hear you
Whispering to one friend
quiz.explanation: Public speaking means sharing with a group, loud and clear enough for everyone to hear.

quiz.question: Where should you look while you talk to a group?
choices: At the people listening
Down at the floor
quiz.explanation: Looking at your listeners helps them feel like you're really talking to them.

quiz.question: Telling about a zoo trip: "first we saw lions, then fed giraffes, then got ice cream." What are the three parts of a story?
choices: A beginning, a middle, and an end
Just a beginning
quiz.explanation: A good story has a beginning, a middle, and an end.

quiz.question: What can help if you feel nervous before talking?
choices: Taking a slow, deep breath
Running away
quiz.explanation: A slow, deep breath can help you feel calmer before you speak.

quiz.question: Why is practicing your words out loud before the big day helpful?
choices: It makes it easier when it's time for real
It makes no difference at all
quiz.explanation: Practicing out loud, even alone, makes the real thing easier.

quiz.question: What can help you remember what to say?
choices: A small card with a picture on it
Nothing can help you remember
quiz.explanation: A small picture card can remind you what to say next.

quiz.question: Should you talk very fast when you feel nervous?
choices: No, talk a little slower
Yes, talk as fast as you can
quiz.explanation: Talking a little slower helps people hear and understand your words.

quiz.question: What should you do if someone asks you a question after you talk?
choices: Listen and answer as best you can
Ignore them and walk away
quiz.explanation: Listening and answering questions politely is part of good public speaking.

slides.title: What makes a good story
slides.text: A good story has a clear beginning, middle, and end. The middle should have something surprising, like a raccoon sneaking into your tent, so people want to keep listening.

slides.title: Practicing out loud
slides.text: Reading your words in your head feels different from saying them out loud. Practicing out loud helps you catch tricky words before the real thing.

slides.title: Practicing before the big day
slides.text: Practicing your talk a few times before the real day helps you feel more confident. Try practicing in front of a family member instead of just alone.

slides.title: Using cue cards
slides.text: A cue card has just a few key words to remind you what comes next. Reading every single word off a card can make your talk sound stiff.

slides.title: Slow down
slides.text: When people get nervous, they often talk faster than they realize. Slowing down on purpose usually sounds just right to your listeners.

slides.title: Pacing yourself
slides.text: Pacing means not rushing through your whole talk at the same fast speed. Slow down for important parts and pause between big ideas.

slides.title: Eye contact with the audience
slides.text: Looking at a few different people while you talk helps everyone feel included. Try not to stare at only your teacher the whole time.

slides.title: Using your hands
slides.text: Simple hand gestures can help explain your idea without needing more words. For example, holding your hands apart shows how big a fish you caught.

slides.title: Speaking loud enough to be heard
slides.text: In a big room, speak louder than feels normal so people in the back can hear you. It's okay to check in by asking if everyone can hear.

slides.title: It's normal to feel nervous
slides.text: Almost everyone feels a little nervous before speaking to a group, even people who do it every day. That nervous feeling doesn't mean something is wrong.

slides.title: Checking they understand
slides.text: Asking "does that make sense?" partway through gives listeners a chance to ask a question. This helps most when you're explaining something tricky, like the rules of a new game.

slides.title: Answering questions with confidence
slides.text: After you finish talking, people may ask questions about what you said. It's okay to pause and think for a second before you answer.

slides.title: What is a "pitch"?
slides.text: A pitch is explaining an idea quickly and saying why it's a good one. Saying "let's play tag because everyone can join" is a mini pitch.

quiz.question: A camping story includes a raccoon sneaking into the tent. What makes a story interesting to listen to?
choices: Something happens in the middle that makes people curious
Nothing happens at all
quiz.explanation: An interesting middle part makes listeners want to know what happens next.

quiz.question: A sentence sounds fine in your head but turns out to be a mouthful when spoken. Why practice out loud instead of just in your head?
choices: It catches tricky parts before the real thing
It doesn't help at all
quiz.explanation: Saying words out loud feels different and reveals parts that need more practice.

quiz.question: When nervous, you feel like you're talking at a normal speed. What are nervous speakers often actually doing?
choices: Talking too fast
Talking too slowly
quiz.explanation: Nervousness often speeds people up without them realizing it.

quiz.question: Why look at a few different classmates while speaking, not just the teacher?
choices: It helps everyone feel included
It's required by law
quiz.explanation: Spreading eye contact around the room helps the whole audience feel included.

quiz.question: Even a teacher who presents daily might feel a few butterflies before a big one. Is it normal to feel nervous before speaking?
choices: Yes, almost everyone does
No, only beginners do
quiz.explanation: Even experienced speakers often feel nervous beforehand.

quiz.question: Saying "let's play tag because everyone can join and it needs no equipment" — what is this an example of?
choices: A pitch — explaining an idea quickly and why it's good
A type of story with no ending
quiz.explanation: A pitch is a quick, convincing explanation of an idea.

quiz.question: Why might reading every single word off a cue card make a talk sound stiff?
choices: A cue card should only have a few key words, not a full script
Cue cards are against the rules
quiz.explanation: Cue cards work best as quick reminders, not something you read word for word.

quiz.question: In a big room, how loud should you speak?
choices: Louder than feels normal, so people in the back can hear
As quietly as possible
quiz.explanation: Speaking louder than usual helps everyone in a big room hear you clearly.

quiz.question: What does pacing yourself while speaking mean?
choices: Not rushing through your whole talk at the same fast speed
Talking as fast as you can the entire time
quiz.explanation: Pacing means slowing down for important parts instead of rushing through everything.

slides.title: Knowing your audience
slides.text: Thinking about who you're talking to — what they already know, and what they care about — helps you decide what to say and how to say it. For example, explaining a video game strategy to friends who already play it needs far less background than explaining the same strategy to a grandparent who's never touched a controller.

slides.title: Structuring a presentation
slides.text: A clear structure — an opening that grabs attention, a few main points, and a short conclusion — is much easier for an audience to follow than jumping around. For example, a book report structured as "here's why I picked this book, here are three key things that happen, here's what I learned" is far easier to follow than jumping randomly between plot points and opinions.

slides.title: Notes vs. memorizing
slides.text: Using a few key-word notes to jog your memory usually sounds more natural than memorizing every word, which can make you freeze if you forget a line. For example, a notecard with just "intro → 3 facts → conclusion" as reminders lets you speak naturally in your own words, unlike memorizing an exact script where forgetting one word can throw you off completely.

slides.title: Managing nervousness
slides.text: Deep breathing, practicing enough times that it feels familiar, and reminding yourself "it's okay to be a little nervous" all genuinely help calm nerves. For example, practicing your presentation out loud five separate times over a few days — not just once the night before — makes the material feel familiar enough that your nerves calm down noticeably by the actual day.

slides.title: Pitching persuasively
slides.text: A persuasive pitch doesn't just explain what an idea is — it explains why the listener should care, in terms that matter to them specifically. For example, pitching a class fundraiser idea to your principal works better if you explain how it benefits the whole school (new playground equipment) rather than just how fun it'll be for your specific class.

slides.title: Keeping visual aids simple
slides.text: A slide or poster with too many words competes with you for attention — a few key words or a picture support what you're saying instead of repeating it. For example, a slide with just a bold headline and one photo, while you explain the details out loud, keeps the audience's attention on you — a slide crammed with paragraphs of text pulls their focus away to reading instead of listening.

slides.title: Handling questions
slides.text: It's okay to pause and think before answering a question, or to say "that's a great question, let me think" instead of rushing an answer. For example, if a classmate asks a tough question you didn't expect during your presentation, pausing for a few seconds to actually think through a good answer looks far more confident than blurting out the first half-formed thought that comes to mind.

slides.title: Pacing your time
slides.text: Practicing with a timer helps you learn whether your presentation is too long, too short, or just right, so you're not rushing through your ending or running out of things to say. For example, if you practice a five-minute presentation and it actually takes eight minutes, you'll know ahead of time to trim a section, instead of realizing it mid-presentation when you notice the teacher checking the clock.

slides.title: Projecting your voice
slides.text: Projecting means speaking from your diaphragm so your voice carries across a room without you needing to shout or strain your throat. For example, standing up straight and taking a breath from your belly before a key sentence lets you say it with real volume and energy, instead of a strained, quiet voice that trails off by the end of the room.

slides.title: Using pauses on purpose
slides.text: A short pause right before or after an important point gives your audience a moment to actually absorb what you just said, instead of rushing straight into the next idea. For example, pausing for a full two seconds after stating your main argument, rather than immediately jumping to your next point, signals to the audience that what you just said matters and deserves a moment to sink in.

slides.title: When something goes wrong
slides.text: Technical problems, like a slide that won't load or a microphone that cuts out, happen to almost every speaker eventually, and staying calm matters more than the problem itself. For example, if your slideshow freezes in the middle of a presentation, calmly saying "give me just a second" while you fix it looks far more professional than panicking or apologizing repeatedly in front of the group.

slides.title: Getting feedback on a practice run
slides.text: Practicing in front of a friend or family member and asking what was confusing or hard to follow catches problems you can't notice by practicing alone. For example, a friend might tell you that you rushed through your third point, or that a certain slide didn't make sense, letting you fix it before the real presentation instead of during it.

quiz.question: Explaining a video game strategy to friends who play it vs. a grandparent who's never touched a controller — why think about your audience first?
choices: It helps you decide what to say and how to say it
The audience never matters
quiz.explanation: Knowing what your audience cares about shapes an effective presentation.

quiz.question: A book report structured as "why I picked it → key events → what I learned." What makes a presentation easy to follow?
choices: A clear opening, main points, and conclusion
Jumping between random ideas
quiz.explanation: A clear structure helps the audience follow along.

quiz.question: A notecard says just "intro → 3 facts → conclusion" instead of a full script. Why might key-word notes work better than memorizing every word?
choices: Forgetting a memorized line can make you freeze
Notes are always required
quiz.explanation: Notes let you speak naturally without the risk of freezing over a forgotten exact word.

quiz.question: Pitching a fundraiser to your principal by explaining school-wide benefits, not just class fun. What makes a pitch persuasive?
choices: Explaining why the listener should care, in terms that matter to them
Using as many words as possible
quiz.explanation: A persuasive pitch connects the idea to what the specific listener cares about.

quiz.question: A slide crammed with paragraphs of text vs. one with a headline and a photo. What's a risk of too many words on a slide?
choices: It competes with you for the audience's attention
It has no effect either way
quiz.explanation: A busy slide can pull attention away from the speaker instead of supporting them.

quiz.question: A classmate asks a tough, unexpected question during your presentation. What's okay to do?
choices: Pause and think before answering
Panic and refuse to answer
quiz.explanation: Taking a moment to think leads to a better answer than rushing.

quiz.question: You practice a five-minute talk and it actually takes eight minutes. Why is timing yourself with a practice run useful?
choices: It shows whether your presentation is too long before the real thing
Timing never matters for a presentation
quiz.explanation: Practicing with a timer lets you trim your presentation ahead of time instead of rushing at the end.

quiz.question: Your slideshow freezes in the middle of your presentation. What's the best way to handle an unexpected technical problem?
choices: Stay calm and say something like "give me a second"
Panic and apologize repeatedly
quiz.explanation: Staying calm during a technical glitch looks far more professional than panicking.

quiz.question: A friend says you rushed through your third point during a practice run. Why is practicing in front of another person useful?
choices: It catches problems you might not notice practicing alone
It has no benefit over practicing alone
quiz.explanation: Another person can point out confusing or rushed parts you can't easily notice by yourself.

slides.title: Reading the room
slides.text: Reading the room means noticing whether your audience looks confused, bored, or engaged while you're speaking, and adjusting on the spot. For example, if several people look lost right after you use a technical term, pausing to explain it simply in the moment keeps the whole room with you, instead of losing them for the rest of the talk.

slides.title: The elevator pitch
slides.text: An elevator pitch explains an idea clearly in about the time of a short elevator ride, forcing you to identify what actually matters most. For example, condensing a whole semester-long project into a 30-second summary — your question, your finding, and why it matters — forces you to find the real heart of your work instead of listing every detail.

slides.title: Credibility: why they trust you
slides.text: Ethos is a fancy word for credibility, meaning the reason an audience decides to trust what you're saying. For example, mentioning that you interviewed three actual teachers before arguing for a longer lunch period gives your speech more ethos than simply stating your opinion.

slides.title: Emotion: why they care
slides.text: Pathos is the term for emotion — using a real story or feeling to make an audience genuinely care about your point. For example, opening a speech about recycling with one specific piece of trash's actual journey creates more pathos than simply stating a fact like "recycling is important."

slides.title: Logic: why it makes sense
slides.text: Logos means logic — the facts, data, and reasoning that make your argument hold up under scrutiny. For example, backing up a school policy argument with real attendance numbers gives it logos, so the case doesn't rest on emotion or trust alone — the strongest speeches usually combine all three.

slides.title: The rule of three
slides.text: The rule of three means grouping ideas into sets of three, since audiences remember and enjoy patterns of three far more than two or four. For example, a speech that says "we need more funding, more staff, and more time" feels more powerful and memorable than listing just two of those, or five.

slides.title: Signposting
slides.text: Signposting means using phrases like "first," "next," and "finally" to show your audience exactly where you are in your talk. For example, saying "my second point is..." out loud helps a listener who briefly zoned out find their place again, instead of feeling lost for the rest of the speech.

slides.title: Storytelling for impact
slides.text: A story with a real setup, a genuine conflict, and a resolution sticks with an audience far longer than a list of facts. For example, opening a speech about recycling with one piece of trash's actual journey, rather than just saying "recycling is important," is far more likely to stick in people's memory.

slides.title: Owning your nerves on stage
slides.text: Even experienced speakers get nervous right before going on stage, and hiding it usually takes more energy than simply accepting it and starting anyway. For example, taking one slow breath backstage and reminding yourself "a little nervous energy is normal" puts that energy to use, instead of trying to suppress it completely.

slides.title: Handling pushback gracefully
slides.text: Responding to a tough or even hostile question calmly, without getting defensive, usually earns more respect than winning the argument would. For example, calmly acknowledging someone's challenge and responding with your reasoning, instead of getting dismissive, earns more respect from the room than "winning" the exchange.

slides.title: Body language and vocal variety
slides.text: Varying your pace, volume, and pauses, instead of speaking in one flat tone, keeps an audience's attention and emphasizes your key points. For example, slowing down and pausing right before your speech's most important sentence makes that point land much harder than saying it in a flat, even tone.

slides.title: Adapting to your time limit
slides.text: A strict time limit forces you to decide which points truly matter and cut the rest, which usually makes a speech stronger, not weaker. For example, if you're given only three minutes instead of five, cutting your weakest example rather than rushing through all of them keeps your strongest points clear.

slides.title: Overcoming stage fright
slides.text: Thorough preparation is the most reliable cure for stage fright — confidence usually comes from knowing your material cold, not a personality trait. For example, someone who looks naturally confident on stage has often just practiced their material so many times that stage fright has little room left to take hold.

slides.title: The call to action
slides.text: A call to action is the specific thing you want your audience to actually do after hearing your speech, not just think about. For example, ending a speech about recycling with "starting tomorrow, bring one reusable bag to school" gives listeners something concrete to act on, instead of just a vague, feel-good idea.

slides.title: Presenting virtually vs. in person
slides.text: Virtual presentations lose most body language cues, so speaking with more vocal energy and checking in verbally matters even more. For example, in person you can glance around and notice confused faces, but on a video call you usually can't, which is why asking "does that make sense?" out loud becomes far more important.

quiz.question: Several audience members look confused after a technical term, and you pause to explain it simply right there. What does "reading the room" let a speaker do?
choices: Adjust in real time based on audience reactions
Ignore the audience completely
quiz.explanation: Noticing audience reactions lets a speaker adapt, like slowing down or adding an example.

quiz.question: Condensing a semester-long project into a 30-second summary of the question, findings, and importance. What is an "elevator pitch"?
choices: A clear explanation of an idea in a very short time
A speech given inside an actual elevator only
quiz.explanation: An elevator pitch forces you to identify what matters most about an idea, briefly.

quiz.question: A speech combines credibility, a real emotional story, and data. Why do persuasive speeches often combine credibility, emotion, and logic?
choices: Relying on just one usually falls flat
Only logic ever matters
quiz.explanation: Blending trust, emotion, and logic is more persuasive than any one alone.

quiz.question: A speech opens with one piece of trash's specific journey, instead of "recycling is important." Why does storytelling stick with an audience better than a list of facts?
choices: A real setup, conflict, and resolution is more memorable
Facts are always more memorable
quiz.explanation: A structured story tends to be far more memorable than a plain list of facts.

quiz.question: Someone aggressively challenges your conclusion, and you calmly acknowledge their point before responding. What usually earns more respect?
choices: Responding calmly without getting defensive
Getting defensive and arguing back
quiz.explanation: A calm, non-defensive response tends to earn more respect than winning an argument.

quiz.question: Slowing down and pausing right before your speech's most important sentence. What does varying your pace, volume, and pauses do for a speech?
choices: Keeps attention and emphasizes key points
Confuses the audience for no reason
quiz.explanation: Vocal variety keeps an audience engaged and highlights what matters most.

quiz.question: Someone who seems naturally confident on stage has usually practiced the material extensively. What is the most reliable cure for stage fright?
choices: Thorough preparation
Just being naturally confident
quiz.explanation: Confidence usually comes from knowing your material well, not an innate trait.

quiz.question: A speech says "we need more funding, more staff, and more time" instead of listing two or five things. What is the "rule of three"?
choices: Grouping ideas into sets of three because audiences remember them well
A rule that speeches must be exactly three minutes long
quiz.explanation: Audiences tend to remember and enjoy patterns of three more than other numbers.

quiz.question: Saying "my second point is..." out loud during a speech. What does signposting help an audience do?
choices: Follow where you are in the talk, even if they briefly zoned out
Guess what your next speech will be about
quiz.explanation: Signposting phrases like "first" and "next" help listeners track your structure.

quiz.question: Ending a recycling speech with "starting tomorrow, bring one reusable bag to school." What is a call to action?
choices: The specific thing you want your audience to actually do
A dramatic way to end any speech
quiz.explanation: A call to action gives listeners something concrete to do after your speech, not just a feeling.
